clinicalPearls: Testicular atrophy describes a testis that has become abnormally small and soft, reflecting loss of seminiferous tubule volume and often impaired spermatogenesis
Causes are diverse and include prior testicular torsion, trauma, orchitis (notably mumps), varicocele, cryptorchidism, previous surgery, and vascular injury
Endocrine and toxic causes include hypogonadotropic states, exogenous androgens or anabolic steroids, and chemotherapy or radiotherapy
Bilateral atrophy raises concern for a systemic, endocrine, or genetic cause such as Klinefelter syndrome, whereas unilateral atrophy often follows a local insult
Assessment includes measurement of testicular volume, a semen analysis when fertility is relevant, and hormone profiling with FSH, LH, and testosterone
An atrophic testis still warrants examination and ultrasound because a small tumour or the increased malignancy risk of an atrophic or previously undescended testis should not be missed
Management is directed at the underlying cause, with attention to fertility preservation, hormone replacement where hypogonadism is confirmed, and counselling
reference.pathophysiology: Testicular atrophy results from injury to or loss of the germinal epithelium and, in some cases, the Leydig cells, leading to shrinkage of testicular volume. Ischaemic insults such as torsion or vascular injury, inflammatory damage from orchitis, the raised scrotal temperature and venous stasis of a varicocele, obstruction or heat effects, direct trauma, and gonadotoxic drugs or radiation all damage the seminiferous tubules. Endocrine causes act by removing the gonadotropin drive needed to maintain the testis, as in hypogonadotropic hypogonadism or suppression by exogenous androgens, while genetic conditions such as Klinefelter syndrome cause progressive tubular sclerosis. The common endpoint is a small, firm-to-soft testis with reduced or absent spermatogenesis.
additionalDifferentials: Klinefelter syndrome and other genetic causes
Cryptorchidism with an intrinsically small testis
additionalInvestigations: Measurement of testicular volume by examination and orchidometer or ultrasound
Scrotal ultrasound to assess parenchyma and exclude a mass
Hormone profile including FSH, LH, and testosterone
Semen analysis when fertility is a concern
Karyotype or genetic testing when a chromosomal cause is suspected
History of medications, anabolic steroid use, and previous gonadotoxic treatment
redFlags: A discrete mass within an atrophic testis suggesting a tumour
Rapid or progressive bilateral atrophy without an obvious cause
Features of hypogonadism such as loss of libido, fatigue, or reduced secondary sexual characteristics
History suggesting an untreated or missed testicular torsion
reference.prognosis: Prognosis depends on the cause and its reversibility: atrophy from established ischaemic, inflammatory, or genetic damage is usually permanent with impaired fertility, whereas atrophy from reversible factors such as varicocele or suppressive drugs may improve when the cause is addressed; hormone replacement can manage hypogonadism.
pitfalls: Overlooking a tumour within a small or previously undescended testis
Attributing atrophy to a single cause without a systematic endocrine and genetic assessment
Missing anabolic steroid use as a reversible contributor
Failing to discuss and arrange fertility preservation before it is too late
references: Campbell-Walsh-Wein Urology, Male Reproductive and Sexual Medicine section
management: Address reversible causes directly, repairing a symptomatic varicocele and withdrawing anabolic steroids or other gonadotoxic agents where possible
Treat hypogonadotropic hypogonadism with gonadotropin therapy using hCG with FSH when fertility is desired, restoring the trophic drive to the testis
Provide androgen replacement with testosterone for symptomatic hypogonadism where fertility is not the immediate goal
Manage fertility with semen analysis, sperm cryopreservation and surgical sperm retrieval with assisted reproduction where indicated
Maintain examination and ultrasound surveillance, since an atrophic or previously undescended testis carries an increased malignancy risk
Arrange karyotyping and genetic counselling where a chromosomal cause such as Klinefelter syndrome is suspected
Coordinate care across urology, endocrinology and fertility services
